articles.title: This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor
articles.author: Allie Skalnik

paras.en: Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

articles.title: This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize
articles.author: Carolyn Gramling

paras.en: The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

articles.title: Drug Restores Liver Function in Aging Rats And Halves Levels of an Alzheimer's-Linked Protein
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: The liver clears substances from our blood, but parts of this system become less efficient as we age.
Scientists have now restored some of that lost function in older rats with an experimental drug, halving blood levels of a protein fragment linked to Alzheimer's disease.
The treatment also lowered cholesterol. After that second finding, the researchers discovered that the drug restored communication between neighboring liver cells.

The study, led by researchers at the University of Southern California, focused on protein fragments that can accumulate as plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer's. Called amyloid-beta, these fragments also circulate in the blood, where the liver helps remove them.
Restoring the aging liver's clearance capacity could therefore lower circulating amyloid-beta, addressing one consequence of aging that might influence disease risk.
"Age is the single greatest risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease," first author and USC liver researcher Sam de Leve told ScienceAlert.

To investigate, the team examined how substances reach the cells responsible for processing them. Much of the amyloid-beta in blood travels attached to fat-carrying particles. Large particles must pass through microscopic openings in the cells lining the liver's small blood vessels to reach its main working cells, called hepatocytes.
As the vessel-lining cells age, these openings become smaller and fewer. The researchers suspected that reopening them would help hepatocytes collect amyloid-beta from the blood.
They gave two-year-old rats an experimental drug called cinaciguat daily for two weeks, comparing them with untreated older rats and four-month-old animals.
The treatment restored the openings. Blood levels of amyloid-beta 40, one form of the protein fragment, fell by half, returning to youthful levels.

LDL, the cholesterol-carrying particles commonly called "bad cholesterol," dropped too. However, LDL particles are small enough to cross the vessel lining even when its openings are lost. Reopening those passages couldn't explain this result.

The team investigated whether the drug also affected communication between cells. They collected liquid in which vessel-lining cells from young or old rats had grown overnight, then added it to hepatocytes from young rats.

Liquid from young cells supported LDL uptake. Liquid from old cells provided no more support than ordinary culture medium. When the older donor rats had received cinaciguat, however, liquid from their cells supported uptake again.

Treatment appeared to have restored a message helping hepatocytes maintain their specialized function. De Leve compared this to a scene in The Lion King: After his father's death, Simba runs from his future as king, until his father, Mufasa, appears to him in spirit.
"It's like Mufasa telling Simba to 'Remember who you are' in The Lion King," de Leve said.

In the liver, that reminder came through a growth factor, a protein that influences cell behavior, called HB-EGF. Older vessel-lining cells still made its precursor but weren't releasing detectable amounts of the soluble signal. Cinaciguat restored that release.
Adding HB-EGF directly to hepatocytes improved their uptake of LDL and amyloid-beta. Blocking it removed the benefits supplied by liquid from young cells.

The hepatocytes offered another clue. Two proteins that capture these substances were present in similar total amounts in older cells, but less of each was at the cell surface, where they work. Treatment restored their surface levels.
The results support a role for HB-EGF in this change, although the researchers didn't directly establish that connection.
De Leve explained that restoring the vessel-lining cells both reopened passages for large molecules and renewed their communication with hepatocytes.

"In youth, the hepatocyte is a specialist at maintaining appropriate circulating levels of LDL cholesterol and amyloid beta, but with aging, the hepatocyte becomes less efficient at clearing those substances," de Leve said.
Whether improving liver clearance could protect the brain remains unknown. Earlier mouse research has linked amyloid produced in the liver to changes in the brain.

This study examined healthy aging, using three to six independent biological samples per condition across different experiments. It didn't establish that treatment reduces brain plaques, improves memory, or prevents Alzheimer's.

The researchers say the approach should next be tested in an animal model of Alzheimer's disease. Developing a human treatment would also require further research into the effectiveness and safety of related drugs.
The research has been published in Journal of Biological Chemistry.

articles.title: 'Good' Body Fat Is Linked to Fewer Anxiety And Depression Diagnoses
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: When we think about body fat, the number on the scale or an expanding waistline often comes to mind.
Research on brown fat is drawing attention to a different connection: patients whose scans showed this tissue had fewer recorded diagnoses of anxiety and depression.

Found in areas including the neck, near the collarbones, and the armpits, brown fat produces heat when activated by cold. It takes up the radioactive sugar tracer used in certain medical scans, making it visible in the images.

"What surprised us the most is that there are no previous studies documenting a potential connection between brown fat and mood," endocrinologist and Rockefeller University researcher Nicolás Gómez-Banoy told ScienceAlert.

The team's 2021 research linked brown fat to lower rates of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Following that study, covered by ScienceAlert, the researchers broadened their investigation to hundreds of diagnoses.

For the research published in Nature, they examined records from more than 100,000 patients at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York. PET/CT scans taken for clinical reasons were assessed alongside patients' diagnoses and medication records.

The team matched patients with and without detectable brown fat on age, sex, body mass index, and outdoor temperature. In these matched groups, depressive episode diagnoses were recorded for 5.4 percent of patients with detectable brown fat and 8.2 percent of those without it. Anxiety disorder diagnoses were also less common in patients with detectable brown fat.
The associations persisted after the analysis accounted for smoking history, cancer type, cancer stage, treatment, and other factors.
The researchers also wanted to know whether the amount and location of active brown fat mattered, so they used artificial intelligence.

A machine learning tool helped measure brown fat volume and glucose uptake in about 8,700 patients with detectable brown fat. Together, these measurements were used to estimate brown fat activity across six body regions.

Higher brown fat activity around the armpits was particularly associated with better cardiovascular and metabolic health. The psychiatric findings came from the separate comparison of recorded diagnoses.
Patients with detectable brown fat also had lower blood sugar measurements, including a marker reflecting longer-term blood sugar levels.

"The most plausible explanation is that patients with brown fat show an improved metabolic profile, healthier fat distribution, and lower inflammatory markers," Gómez-Banoy explained. "All of these things have been linked to improved psychiatric outcomes."

Patients taking certain antidepressants in the SSRI class, used to treat depression and anxiety, were less likely to have detectable brown fat. The association remained after the researchers adjusted for relevant psychiatric diagnoses and was consistent with earlier human research showing that these medications can reduce brown fat activity.

The team also searched medication records for drugs that might activate brown fat. Patients taking certain blood pressure medications were more likely to have detectable tissue. The researchers tested one of them, losartan, in laboratory-grown brown fat cells and mice.
Losartan increased brown fat activity, and treated mice expended more energy. These experiments did not evaluate anxiety or depression.
"Given that our study is retrospective, it is important to note that these findings are associations and do not demonstrate causation," Gómez-Banoy said.

The study drew on patients at a cancer center, and more than three-quarters of those in the matched groups were women. The paper also notes that tumor types and cancer treatments differed between the groups. Their influence on the findings cannot be ruled out despite statistical adjustments.
Gómez-Banoy said trials of drugs or other methods to activate brown fat should also record whether patients' anxiety or depression changes.
The research has been published in Nature.

articles.title: MIT Scientists Break a 20-Year Rule And Unlock Never-Before-Seen Crystal Structures
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: One of the key methods through which scientists develop and enhance new materials is by getting more control over their structure at the smallest scales, and microscopic nanoparticles can be incredibly useful for this kind of detail.
Now researchers led by a team from MIT have overturned the conventional thinking of the last couple of decades when it comes to how these nanoparticles are connected together.
Previously, the connectors – or ligands – between the nanoparticles have mostly been designed as rigid and fixed.
In a new study in Nature Materials, the researchers went for the opposite approach, building connector molecules that were floppy rather than rigid.
The nature of the links is determined by the nanoparticles themselves as they come together.

Crucially, the researchers found that this gave them better control over the number of links between the nanoparticles, and the direction of those links. And with better control, comes more possibilities for new materials.

"People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into," says materials scientist Rob Macfarlane, from MIT.
"This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn't been investigated before. It's exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive."

Materials made of nanoparticles are already widely used in a variety of fields, but they can be difficult to scale up. By default, they pack together tightly and have to be carefully engineered for each specific purpose.

Here, the researchers used gold nanoparticles with ligands made from a common, floppy polymer called PEG, tipped with positive or negative charges to aid the connections. Computer simulations were also run to follow what the experiment was showing.

Without any rigidity, the ligands ended up bunching together where the particles touched, which in turn limited the number of connections that could be made – there were only so many particle-to-particle chains to go around.
"It's the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail," says Macfarlane.
"We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well."

The connections can still be controlled to a large extent by changing the sizes of the nanoparticles and the lengths of the ligand chains. For example, the team found that smaller particles led to fewer links.

In tests, the team was able to create ordered crystal structures that haven't been seen before. The functionality of these materials still needs to be examined and tested, but the results of the experiment are promising.
"Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has," says Macfarlane.
"The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before."

Materials scientists have previously tried to fine-tune nanoparticle connections by precisely aligning them, or changing the shape of the particles themselves. It turns out that relinquishing some rigidity actually brings about more order.

According to the researchers, the new approach could lead to the development of high-performance materials in fields including photonics (technologies that control light), chemical catalysis, medicine, and agriculture.

Ultimately, nanoparticles that aren't packed as closely together mean a material that can be customized at scale more easily, and "that's where a lot of the interesting applications are," says Macfarlane.
The next steps will be to experiment with other particle materials and ligand combinations, and put the materials to the test in real scenarios.

"If you know what your building blocks are and how they're arranged, you can explain what properties materials have," says Macfarlane. "Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties."
The research has been published in Nature Materials.

articles.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots

paras.en: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots

- Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

North Carolina's blueberry growers are facing an emerging threat from a destructive beetle whose larvae feed underground, damaging plant roots and potentially killing blueberry bushes. Scientists have now identified the insect responsible, providing an important first step toward protecting crops from the pest.

A research team at North Carolina State University has confirmed that the culprit is Prionus imbricornus, a species of longhorn beetle distinguished by its long antennae. These wood-boring insects are becoming a growing concern for blueberry producers in the state.

Female beetles generally deposit their eggs in soil near the roots of hardwood trees. After hatching, the larvae feed on the roots, sometimes destroying enough tissue to kill the tree. The larvae can reach an impressive five inches in length, while the adult beetles do not feed.
A Decade-Old Mystery Beneath Blueberry Fields

North Carolina is the first state to document P. imbricornus feeding on blueberry bushes. However, signs of a similar problem have existed for years. Reports of unidentified Prionus larvae damaging blueberry roots date back to 2010, but researchers had struggled to determine which species was responsible.

Part of the challenge was the insects' underground habitat. Because the larvae remain near plant roots, they are difficult to locate and study. Making matters more complicated, larvae from different longhorn beetle species often look remarkably similar, making visual identification unreliable.

According to Kenneth Geisert, a graduate student in NC State's College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and lead author of the study, this uncertainty has made it difficult to develop appropriate pest control strategies.

"Before now, researchers often just assumed the species of Prionus on their commodities based on adult identification," Geisert said. "If that guess was incorrect, it could mean using a treatment strategy that did not line up with the problem and incorrectly associating species and their hosts. For instance, while P. imbricornus attacks roots, another type of longhorn beetle might attack the trunk of a tree, or dead branches. Without knowing which species of beetle you're dealing with and their ecology, incorrect management can cause adverse effects on non-target insects."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To identify the insects, the research team conducted fieldwork at six blueberry farms in North Carolina's Pender, Sampson, Bladen, and New Hanover counties.

The scientists installed black panel traps containing sex pheromones, chemical signals that attract adult beetles. After collecting the insects, they used a DNA identification technique known as genetic barcoding to determine the identity of larvae found in the fields.

This method examines short, standardized sections of DNA and compares them with reference sequences from known species. By matching genetic material from the unidentified larvae with DNA from adult Prionus beetles, the researchers could determine which species was present.
The analysis produced a 98 to 99 percent match with P. imbricornus, confirming the identity of the beetle responsible for the root damage.
A Growing Threat With No Approved Insecticides
Although identifying the pest represents an important breakthrough, it also highlights a serious challenge for blueberry growers.

Lorena Lopez, an assistant extension professor in NC State's Department of Entomology and Plant Pathology and a co-author of the study, explained that the discovery brings both encouraging and troubling news.

"On one hand, it's very important that we know which species we're dealing with," she said. "On the other, North Carolina was the first state to ever report Prionus infestation in blueberries, and there are no insecticides currently labeled against this pest in blueberries."
To help address this problem, Lopez has begun testing insecticides to determine which treatments might effectively control the beetles.

A major focus is finding the best time to apply treatments. By coordinating insecticide applications with the beetles' reproductive cycles, researchers hope to disrupt larval development before the insects can inflict extensive damage on blueberry roots.
If successful, this approach could give farmers a much-needed way to protect their crops against an emerging pest that has remained difficult to identify and manage for more than a decade.

The findings appear in the Journal of Integrated Pest Management in a paper titled "Prionus imbricornis (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), an emerging pest in North Carolina blueberries." Gareth Powell, an assistant professor at NC State and director of the NCSU Insect Museum, also contributed to the research.

articles.title: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

paras.en: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

- A study of nearly 5,800 adults found that heart scans measuring calcium buildup in the arteries led to the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, despite recommending statins to far fewer patients. Surprisingly, patients advised to take statins based on their scans were nearly three times as likely to stick with their medication, raising intriguing questions about how doctors should identify and treat heart disease risk.

A major clinical trial has raised new questions about how doctors decide who should take statins to prevent heart attacks and strokes. Researchers found that using heart scans to guide treatment decisions produced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, even though the scans led to far fewer recommendations to begin taking statins.

The findings, presented during a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026, also revealed a striking difference in how consistently patients took their medication. Those advised to use statins based on calcium buildup in their coronary arteries were substantially more likely to follow their treatment recommendations.

Although the results suggest that heart scans could help doctors make more targeted treatment decisions, the trial did not establish that the scan approach was as effective as conventional risk assessment. Researchers say additional studies are needed to determine whether it offers a better strategy for preventing cardiovascular disease.
Why Predicting Heart Disease Risk Remains a Challenge

Cardiovascular disease remains the world's leading cause of illness and death. Much of this burden comes from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), which develops when fatty deposits known as plaque accumulate inside arteries, restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke are two major forms of this condition.

Several common factors increase the likelihood of developing ASCVD, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and elevated cholesterol. Doctors use these factors to estimate a person's cardiovascular risk and determine whether preventive medications are appropriate.

Statins are among the most widely used treatments for lowering that risk. These medications reduce cholesterol levels, particularly low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called LDL or bad cholesterol. They also help lower the likelihood of serious cardiovascular complications.

However, identifying which patients stand to benefit from statins remains a significant challenge. Some people who eventually experience a heart attack do not appear to be at particularly high risk under conventional screening methods.

"For far too many patients, the first symptom of ASCVD is a heart attack," said Doctor Joseph B Muhlestein from the Intermountain Medical Center, Murray, USA, the Principal Investigator of the CorCal Outcomes trial. "Statins have been shown to be highly effective in the prevention of ASCVD; however, there is a major gap in risk assessment, statin initiation, and statin persistence."

According to Muhlestein, many people who suffer their first heart attack, particularly younger adults, would not previously have been classified as having enough cardiovascular risk to justify statin treatment. This limitation has prompted researchers to investigate whether directly examining the arteries might provide more useful information.
Can Heart Calcium Scans Improve Statin Decisions?
The CorCal Outcomes trial investigated two different approaches for determining which patients should be advised to begin statin therapy before experiencing a cardiovascular event.

The first relied on the pooled cohort equations (PCE), a commonly used risk assessment tool that estimates cardiovascular risk using traditional factors such as age, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and smoking status.
The second approach measured coronary artery calcium (CAC), which provides a more direct indication of plaque buildup in the arteries supplying the heart.

This measurement uses a computed tomography (CT) scan to detect calcium deposits in the coronary arteries. Calcium can accumulate within atherosclerotic plaque, making it a useful marker of underlying coronary artery disease, even in people who have not developed symptoms.

Unlike traditional risk calculators, which estimate the likelihood of future cardiovascular problems based on personal characteristics and health measurements, calcium scans provide evidence of disease already present in the coronary arteries.
Researchers wanted to determine whether using this information to guide statin recommendations could improve cardiovascular outcomes.
Nearly 5,800 Patients Put Both Methods to the Test

The trial enrolled 5,772 patients from the Canyons and Desert regions of Intermountain Health Care in the United States. Participants had no known history of ASCVD or diabetes and had not previously received statin therapy.
Their average age was 64, and women accounted for 51% of the study population.

Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to one of two groups. One group received statin treatment guidance based on traditional cardiovascular risk scores, while the other received recommendations based on coronary calcium scan results.

Both patients and their physicians were informed of the treatment recommendations generated by the study protocol. However, the final decision about whether to start taking statins remained with the patients and their doctors.
The researchers then tracked major cardiovascular events (MACE; all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and arterial revascularization).
This combined outcome included death from any cause, heart attacks, strokes, and procedures to restore blood flow through narrowed or blocked arteries.
Heart Scans Led to Far Fewer Statin Recommendations
After an average follow-up of 4.2 years, researchers found that major cardiovascular events occurred at exactly the same observed rate in both groups.

A total of 2.7% of patients in each group experienced one of the events included in the study's primary outcome. The estimated relative risk over time was also nearly identical (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% confidence interval 0.71 to 1.38; p=0.045 for noninferiority).

However, this similarity did not establish that the two strategies were equally effective. The study failed to meet its predetermined statistical requirement for demonstrating that the calcium scan approach was not meaningfully worse than conventional risk assessment.
A notable difference emerged in how frequently patients were advised to begin taking statins.

Participants evaluated using traditional risk scores received recommendations to start statin therapy more than three times as often as those whose decisions were guided by coronary calcium measurements.
Despite this substantial difference in treatment recommendations, both groups experienced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events during the follow-up period.
A Surprising Difference in Statin Adherence
Perhaps the most intriguing finding involved whether patients actually followed their prescribed treatment.

Among those advised to take statins, patients whose recommendations were based on calcium scans were much more likely to adhere to their medication regimen than those assessed using traditional cardiovascular risk factors.
The difference was substantial (62% vs. 23%).
In other words, patients recommended statins based on visible evidence of calcium buildup in their arteries were approximately 2.7 times as likely to follow their medication regimen.

One possible explanation is that seeing evidence of disease in their own arteries makes patients more motivated to take preventive medication. However, the trial did not establish why adherence differed so dramatically between the groups.

The findings raise the possibility that coronary calcium scans could influence not only which patients receive statin recommendations, but also whether those patients consistently take the medications.
What the Findings Mean for Heart Disease Prevention

Despite these potentially important differences, the researchers emphasized that the study could not establish whether calcium scan-guided treatment provides cardiovascular protection comparable to traditional risk assessment.

One important limitation was that fewer participants experienced major cardiovascular events than the investigators had anticipated. With fewer events to analyze, the trial had less statistical power to determine whether a meaningful difference existed between the two approaches.

"The power of the study to detect a difference was reduced by the lower-than-expected event rates and we did not demonstrate noninferiority between the groups," said Doctor Muhlestein, who concluded: "The study did provide important hypothesis-generating insights into the efficiency of statin initiation and adherence when decisions are based on CAC scoring. Taken together, our data could be used to plan an additional well-powered randomized trial comparing CAC with current risk factor-based algorithms."

paras.en: The findings may help researchers design future trials capable of determining whether coronary calcium scans can improve the efficiency of statin prescribing without compromising cardiovascular protection.

Current European recommendations already recognize a potential role for these measurements. The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidemias recommends considering increased coronary calcium scores, when available, as an additional factor in cardiovascular risk assessment.
This guidance applies particularly to people at moderate cardiovascular risk or those whose estimated risk falls near the threshold at which preventive medication would normally be recommended.
For these individuals, evidence of calcium buildup may help doctors make more informed decisions when the need for statin therapy is uncertain.

The CorCal Outcomes findings add to the discussion by suggesting that heart scans may also influence how faithfully patients follow treatment. Whether that advantage translates into better long-term cardiovascular outcomes remains an important question for future research.

articles.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

paras.en: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

- Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.
Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.
"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."
How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.
In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.
A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.
Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.
"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.
"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.
Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.
"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.
The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

articles.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
articles.author: Robert Lea

paras.en: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star.

The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight.
The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight.

"For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement. "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden."

There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight.
The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem.
Telescopes their more stable digital twins

The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors.

This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image.

To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets.

The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image-processing techniques two to 15 times. This led to ERI b emerging from data collected by the JWST two years ago.

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn't see," Wang said. "This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way."
The team hopes that FLIP can now be adopted by other astronomers in a bid to recover hitherto undiscovered exoplanets that have been hidden by the glare of their stars.
This could be a major boon for NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars.

"We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system," team leader Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez of Northwestern University said. "It's not that they don’t exist. It's that we cannot see them.

"Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is."
The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Nature.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.author: Jamie Carter

paras.en: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned.

I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way. Would she like to see it?

She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied.

There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece.

That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects.

I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31.

You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle.

There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense.

I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. They gather enough light to make the galaxy's bright central region much more obvious without turning the exercise into a technical one.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A really useful skill here — whether looking unaided or through binoculars — is averted vision. Instead of staring directly at the galaxy, look slightly beside it. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. It feels slightly ridiculous the first time you do it — deliberately not looking at the thing you're trying to see — but it works.

If light pollution means you need binoculars, that still counts. No one gets a prize for detecting Andromeda unaided. After all, the extraordinary part isn't how you see it. It's what the light has done before reaching you. When those photons began their journey, modern humans did not exist. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor.

This is the week you've been waiting for if you want to spend time on faint objects rather than fighting moonlight. Without a bright moon overhead, spend some time on Andromeda, but revisit the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884). Binoculars show it beautifully, and unlike M31, it becomes more obviously crowded with stars as you increase magnification. Two other large, bright open star clusters in this region that look great in 10x50 binoculars are the glittering stars of NGC 752 in Andromeda and M34, a bright, hazy patch in Perseus.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Also keep an eye out for "shooting stars" because the Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 11-12. Rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — so don't expect them to "light up the night sky". But they can produce bright, long-lasting 'fireballs' that can add a bit of pizzazz to a stargazing session.

Now that you've found its jewel, the Andromeda galaxy, it's worth trying to construct the constellation itself. As with M31, start with the Great Square of Pegasus and Alpheratz at its northeastern corner. Although it looks like part of the square, Alpheratz actually belongs to Andromeda. From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

articles.title: See the space race like you’ve never seen it before in PBS’s new living documentary, ‘We Chose to Go to the Moon’
articles.author: Jeff Spry

paras.en: Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch.
"We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy."

With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen.

These roles include astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins and Ed White, Mission Control trailblazer Poppy Northcutt, "Hidden Figures" mathematician Katherine Johnson and members of the spacefaring families that remained on Earth, including Janet Armstrong and Betty Grissom.

This dynamic multimedia production is directed by Tony Award winner Michael Mayer ("Chess"), combining a unique fusion of theater, concert and documentary storytelling using rare archival footage alongside historic flags and artifacts taken to the Moon and returned home. It also revisits the ill-fated Apollo 13 mission and adds a special tribute to moonwalker Neil Armstrong performed by his son Mark and granddaughter Kali.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" is created, written and narrated by historian John Monsky and stars Ian Weinberger ("Hamilton"), Skylar Astin ("Pitch Perfect"), Brent Comer ("The Outsiders"), Claybourne Elder ("Company"), Elizabeth Gillies (Netflix's "Dynasty"), Taylor Louderman ("Mean Girls") and Joy Woods ("Galileo"). Finally, Ian Weinberger ("Chess," "Hamilton") pulls it all together by conducting Broadway vocalists and the Orchestra of St. Luke’s in a selection of popular period music showcasing songs such as "Fly Me to the Moon," "Rocket Man," "Space Oddity" and "Sound of Silence."

articles.title: Flexell Space and Satoro Agree to Collaborate on In-Orbit Demonstration of Next-Generation Space Solar Cells
articles.author: Flexell Space

paras.en: – Two demonstration missions planned aboard SpaceX Falcon 9, one each in 2027 and 2028
– Satoro to provide “Satellite-as-a-service” solution; Flexell Space to supply solar cells and test modules

Uiwang-si, Korea – Flexell Space, a space energy company led by CEO Taehun Ahn, announced that it has signed an agreement with Singapore-based CubeSat specialist Satoro, led by CEO Mark Lu, for the in-orbit demonstration and validation (IOD/IOV) of next-generation space solar cells.

The agreement aims to verify the performance and reliability of Flexell Space’s solar cells in the actual space environment. The companies plan to conduct two demonstration missions, one in 2027 and another in 2028. Each demonstration satellite is scheduled to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

Flexell Space previously conducted two space demonstration missions through launches aboard Korea’s KSLV-II, in November 2025 and October 2026. Building on this experience, the agreement with Satoro will expand opportunities for in-orbit validation of its next-generation space solar cells and support the continued accumulation of operational data needed for commercialization.

Under the agreement, Satoro will manufacture the satellites for the demonstration missions, while Flexell Space will supply the solar cells and test modules to be integrated into them. The companies will coordinate technical requirements for the CubeSat platforms and demonstration payloads, working together to evaluate the solar cells’ operating characteristics and performance in orbit.

Through these missions, Flexell Space plans to compare and validate ground-test results against in-orbit operational data and assess the solar cells’ power output characteristics and performance changes over time. Data collected from both missions will support further design improvements and reliability validation, strengthening the technical foundation for evaluations by global customers and future commercial supply.

The collaboration brings together Satoro’s expertise in CubeSat manufacturing and demonstration missions with Flexell Space’s capabilities in next-generation solar cell development. Flexell Space is developing solar cell technologies based on CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) and perovskites, with a focus on commercializing low-cost, large-area, ultralight power solutions for satellites and a wide range of space infrastructure.

“Commercializing space solar cells requires both ground-based performance validation and data collected in orbit,” said Taehun Ahn, CEO of Flexell Space. “With two demonstration opportunities secured for 2027 and 2028, we will systematically verify the performance and reliability of our next-generation solar cells and build the technical evidence required by global customers.”
He added, “Our collaboration with Satoro establishes a clear path from development to in-orbit demonstration and will accelerate our preparations for future commercial supply.”

“We are pleased to work with Flexell Space on the demonstration of its next-generation space solar cells,” said Mark Lu, CEO of Satoro. “Drawing on Satoro’s CubeSat platforms and mission integration capabilities, we will work closely with Flexell Space to help secure the in-orbit data needed to validate its technology.”

He added, “We look forward to these two demonstration missions advancing the commercial potential of new space power technologies and laying the groundwork for continued technical collaboration between our companies.”

Flexell Space is a space energy company that originated as an internal venture at Hanwha Systems and develops next-generation space solar cells and power solutions. The company focuses on low-cost, large-area, ultralight products based on CIGS and perovskite solar cell technologies, with an emphasis on the durability, radiation tolerance, and long-term operational reliability required for space applications. Through collaboration with global satellite manufacturers and space agencies, Flexell Space is advancing the commercialization of solar cell technologies for satellites and space infrastructure.

articles.title: How to Expand Reliable, Flexible Access to Space
articles.author: Exolaunch

paras.en: The space industry launched more rockets into orbit last year than ever before, yet satellite operators are confronting an unexpected problem: There still aren’t enough rides to go around.
And increasingly, the shortage isn’t simply about the number of rockets.

Satellite companies want launches to more orbital destinations, with more regularity and aboard a wider range of vehicles. Instead, much of the industry has come to depend on a relatively small number of frequently launched rockets that often go to similar orbits. That’s left some companies and their spacecraft waiting months or years for a suitable ride.

“Demand is crazy,” said Robert Sproles, chief executive of Exolaunch, a Berlin-based broker of global launch services that has put 912 satellites into orbit during 51 separate launch events. “The demand curve is so much steeper than the supply curve.”

The squeeze comes despite a historic expansion in launch activity. Data from the FAA shows the agency licensed 187 launches in fiscal year 2026. That’s up from less than 100 a decade earlier and governments are pushing for still more. The Trump administration has called for U.S. spaceports to support more than 1,000 launches and reentries annually by 2030.

But raw launch numbers obscure a problem that is becoming increasingly important as the space economy grows. A rocket going to the wrong orbit at the wrong time isn’t necessarily useful to a satellite operator.
All of that is turning choice, not just capacity, into one of the launch industry’s biggest constraints.
In order to truly close the gap between supply and demand, Sproles said, space transportation companies must also increase the diversity of available launches.

“Yes, we need to meet demand. But we also need to make sure we’re putting that demand in the right places,” he said. “We need to recognize what types of launches are best for what types of missions, and we need to make sure those types of launches are available when the launch customer needs them.”

Market research firm Novaspace reports that the global space economy reached a valuation of $626 billion in 2025. Citing “consolidation, integration, and closer institutional alignment around security, resilience, and operational performance,” it forecasts annual growth of 5.5% through 2034 — at which point it predicts the global space economy will be worth over $1 trillion.
Markets that large are not monolithic, Sproles said, which means the industry needs multiple launch providers operating regularly across different orbital regimes.

“If you rewind to, say, 2016, there was more launch diversity in the market at that time than there is today. There was not more capacity, but there was a wider variety of vehicles that you could reliably gain access to,” Sproles said. The reasons for that decline in launch diversity includes changes in technology, geopolitics, and supply chains since the COVID-19 pandemic, all of which have led to the concentration of launch capacity in a small number of highly active launch providers.
But that variety is necessary, Sproles argues, because launch customers want to be able to optimize for when they can launch, where they need to go, and how much it will cost.

Consider the two most prolific launch providers today: SpaceX — whose Falcon 9 vehicle is optimized for large commercial constellations, human spaceflight, and heavy commercial rideshares — and Rocket Lab, whose Electron vehicle favors small satellites and CubeSats that require custom orbital planes.

“You could not come up with two more different vehicles both in terms of performance and commercial offerings, which just goes to show you that the industry is as hungry for choice as it is for capacity,” Sproles said.

In today’s launch market, rideshare services are a foundation of the space industry. “Rideshare is appropriate when your schedule is flexible enough to align with when a planned rideshare is launching, and when you have enough orbital wiggle room to go where the masses want to go,” Sproles said. “Basically, it makes sense when you have less rigid mission constraints.”

But as missions become more complex and bespoke, one size doesn’t fit all. Rideshare alternatives are needed, including shared launches — where launches are conceived from the outset with multiple customers in mind, instead of one customer’s mission piggybacking haphazardly onto another’s — and dedicated launches, wherein a customer procures an entire launch that’s customized to their unique schedule, destination, and payload, Sproles said
Exolaunch points to four planned missions that underscore the benefits of launch diversity:
- In 2027, the company will conduct a mid-inclination rideshare mission aboard Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ H3 rocket. It will be the company’s first launch from Japan.

- In late 2027 and 2028, respectively, Exolaunch will launch its Exo-1 and Exo-2 missions aboard two dedicated SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets procured exclusively for an anchor customer that in both instances will use approximately 40% of the launch vehicle; Exolaunch will sell the remaining 60% to other customers seeking a rideshare model.

- In late 2028, Exolaunch will serve as the launch co-integrator for the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment-Continuity (GRACE-C) mission that is a joint effort of the German Space Agency’s German Aerospace Center (DLR) and NASA. The company will provide a custom structure with which to secure the mission’s payload inside a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that DLR and NASA had already secured for their launch; in return, DLR and NASA will allow it to provide the rocket’s unused capacity to other customers.
